Experiments were conducted at the U.S. Air Force's Turbine Research Facility (TRF), a transient blow-down facility with a full-scale, high-speed, fully-cooled vane and rotor stage.
Measurements of pressure, temperature, and heat flux were taken at flow conditions matched to actual engine operation.
The researchers focused on the tip/shroud region of the rotor stage and the high-pressure turbine vane.
The primary goal was to understand the unsteady flow effects, particularly the high-frequency events associated with the blade passage frequency.
The researchers used the Popp method to determine the film cooling parameters of heat transfer coefficient and adiabatic effectiveness from the experimental data.
The angled, fan-shaped coolant holes were designed to provide immediate downstream coverage and width-wise coverage along the airfoil surface.
Significant unsteady pressure and temperature variations were observed on the vane suction surface and rotor shroud due to the interaction between the vane wake and rotor blades.
The unsteady effects resulted in noticeable variations in heat flux on both the vane suction surface and the rotor shroud, impacting the film cooling effectiveness.
The full-scale, high-speed facility allowed the researchers to capture the unsteady effects that are present in actual engine operating conditions.
Time-resolved data analysis techniques like FFTs and ensemble averaging were used to isolate the unsteady pressure and temperature variations.
The researchers found that tip flow and vane wake-rotor interaction result in noticeable heat flux variations in time.
Understanding the unsteady effects on film cooling is crucial for improving engine reliability and durability by mitigating high-cycle fatigue.
The researchers recommended further investigation into the specific mechanisms driving the unsteady effects and the impact of different film cooling schemes.
The study was conducted on a full-scale, high-speed, fully-cooled turbine vane and rotor stage of proprietary design.
Measurements were taken at flow conditions non-dimensionally matched to actual engine operation.
